thread.title: Stock gains in 2018 aren’t just a tech story, but they’re mostly a tech story - MarketWatch

author: Ryan Vlastelica
title: Stock gains in 2018 aren’t just a tech story, but they’re mostly a tech story - MarketWatch
text:
The U.S. stock market has been mostly bounding higher of late, with the Nasdaq hitting a record on Thursday and other major indexes on track for the fifth rise of the past six sessions. Investors shouldn’t be fooled, however. Although, stocks have broadly been doing well, the gains are much narrower than may be apparent at first blush.
The rally in stocks is heavily due to pronounced outperformance in just a few names. Because these companies are among the largest on Wall Street, they have an outsize impact on the broader impact.
As has been the case for months , the gainers are largely within the FAANG group of stocks, an acronym that refers to Facebook FB, +1.86% Apple AAPL, +1.60% Amazon AMZN, +2.28% Netflix NFLX, -1.49% and Google-parent Alphabet Inc. GOOGL, +2.43% All five are in the technology or internet space, as Amazon and Netflix are technically classified as consumer-discretionary stocks.
In a sign of how much the market has been tracking such stocks, correlation between the tech and consumer-discretionary sectors has been extremely high. According to DataTrek Research, the technology sector has had a correlation of 0.86 with the S&P 500 over the past month. Perfect correlation between the two—meaning that whatever one does, the other will match—would be expressed as a reading of 1.0. The discretionary sector has a correlation of 0.87.
All five of the FAANG companies—along with other tech bellwethers like Microsoft MSFT, +2.05% —have outperformed the S&P 500 SPX, +0.80% thus far this year, sometimes significantly so. Amazon, for example, is up more than 50% thus far in 2018, while Netflix has more than doubled. The S&P 500 is up 4.5%.
According to Ben Carlson, a portfolio manager at Ritholtz Wealth Management, Amazon by itself accounts for more than a third—35%—of the S&P 500’s year-to-date return. Netflix accounts for 21% of the S&P’s advance, while Microsoft and Apple together account for 27%.
In other words, more than half the year-to-date gain of the broader market in 2018 can be credited to just two stocks, and more than 80% is due to four stocks. If you extend this to the six biggest boosts—Alphabet and Facebook each account for 8% of the S&P’s move higher—that swells to 99%. Remove these six names, and the market is essentially flat on the year.
“The obvious takeaway here would seem to be that 2018 market returns are all being driven by a handful of names. And if that handful of stocks ever come back down to earth, which they’ve been wont to do on occasion, watch out below,” Carlson wrote in a blog post, calling the outsize contribution of these names “absurdly high.”
Read: One of 2018’s most successful stock plays may be about to turn
He wasn’t the only analyst to cite this issue as a potential warning sign for the market.
Lisa Shalett, head of investment and portfolio strategies for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, noted that the “relatively benign” year-to-date returns were “concentrated in a few stocks” whose gains were “not representative of the challenges most investors have faced.”
She added, “narrowing breadth is an outcome of a market where financial conditions are deteriorating from the mix of Fed tightening, expanding U.S. deficits, higher inflation, strong oil prices, widening credit spreads and a resurgent U.S. dollar.”
Such “extreme performance divergences will likely close,” Shalett wrote, “rewarding year-to-date laggards at the expense of winners.”
That a select tech stalwarts have been leading the market’s advance doesn’t necessarily mean that other stocks are falling. The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF RSP, +0.52% —an exchange-traded fund that equally weights every component of the S&P 500, as opposed to organizing them by market value—is up 3.1% thus far this year. While that is below the 4.6% gain of the capitalization-weighted S&P 500, it indicates that the average move of a component has been positive.
A similar trend can be seen using another ETF that flips the benchmark. The Reverse Cap Weighted US Large Cap ETF RVRS, +0.18% wherein the largest stocks in the index have the least weight and the smallest have the most , is up 3.4% in 2018.
In addition to tech, the other big gainer of 2018 has been the Russell 2000 index RUT, +0.28% of small capitalization shares, which has benefited from a high level of exposure to domestic revenue. This has insulated small stocks from both uncertainty surrounding trade policy and the rising U.S. dollar DXY, +0.08% which can act as a headwind on multinational stocks.
The Russell 2000 is up 10.2% thus far this year.
Ryan Vlastelica Ryan Vlastelica is a markets reporter for MarketWatch and is based in New York. Follow him on Twitter @RyanVlastelica.
